w: Estimates of its scroll count swing from 40,000 to 700,000, but either way this was where the ancient world came to think. Eratosthenes measured the Earth's circumference here; Callimachus wrote what may be the first library catalog ever made. Nothing physical remains, only the legend of what was lost.
_facts: Part of the Mouseion research institution; estimates of its scroll holdings range from 40,000 to 700,000
Scholars there included Eratosthenes (measured Earth's circumference) and Callimachus (wrote the Pinakes, an early library catalog)
No physical structure survives today

w: Named for a 13th-century Sufi mystic buried here alongside members of the Ashraf family, this mosque doubles as mausoleum and shrine. It shares one courtyard with two neighbours, the Al-Busiri and Sidi Yaqut Al-Arsh mosques, all three facing each other across the same sahn in the Anfoushi quarter.
s: A Sufi mystic's tomb, mosque and shrine in one
_facts: 13th-century mosque, mausoleum and Sufi shrine in the Anfoushi neighbourhood
Named for and burial place of Abu'l Abbas al-Mursi, a 13th-century mystic, along with the Ashraf family
Shares a central courtyard (sahn) with the adjacent Al-Busiri and Sidi Yaqut Al-Arsh mosques

w: Despite the name, this granite column has nothing to do with Pompey, it honours emperor Diocletian, raised around 298-302 AD and once topped by a statue of him in armour. It stands in the ruined precinct of the Serapeum, a temple Ptolemy III built for the god Serapis, which held a daughter library to the Great Library.
s: A Roman column named for the wrong Roman entirely
_facts: Roman triumphal column raised 298-302 AD in honour of emperor Diocletian, despite its modern name
Stands within the ruined temenos of the Serapeum of Alexandria, a temple Ptolemy III built for the god Serapis
The Serapeum once housed a daughter library of the Library of Alexandria; plundered by Christians in the late 4th century

w: Nobody found this necropolis on purpose, a donkey stumbled into the access shaft in 1900 and opened up tombs cut into the bedrock centuries earlier. A spiral staircase once carried bodies down to chambers where Egyptian, Greek and Roman styles blur together. One hall even holds the bones of an emperor's horses.
s: Discovered when a donkey fell through the ground
_facts: Necropolis tunneled into bedrock during the Antonine period (2nd century CE), used as a burial chamber into the 4th century
Rediscovered in 1900 when a donkey fell into the access shaft
Statues blend Egyptian, Greek and Roman styles; the Hall of Caracalla contains the bones of that emperor's horses

w: Sultan Qaitbay raised this fortress between 1477 and 1479 on the spot where the Pharos, one of the Seven Wonders, had stood for over a millennium before earthquakes brought it down. Its walls used some of the lighthouse's own fallen stones, the last great wonder recycled into the next one.
s: Built from the stones of the Lighthouse of Alexandria
_facts: 15th-century defensive fortress built 1477-1479 AD by Sultan Al-Ashraf Sayf al-Din Qaitbay
Stands at the mouth of the Eastern Harbour, on the site of the ruined Pharos lighthouse
Some of its stones came from the fallen lighthouse, which had used the same site until the 1480s

w: Built on a low plateau east of the city centre, this palace and museum look straight down onto a private stretch of Mediterranean coastline. Its extensive gardens gave the whole surrounding district its name and its holiday character, the grounds now among the most photographed green spaces in Alexandria.
s: A royal retreat perched over its own private beach
_facts: Palace, museum and gardens on a plateau overlooking a Mediterranean beach in Alexandria's Montaza district
Gave its name to the surrounding Montaza neighbourhood
East of central Alexandria, functions today as museum plus public gardens

w: This is the historical seat of the Pope of Alexandria, head of the Coptic Orthodox Church, a line running back through centuries of the Coptic papacy. In April 2017 it was the target of a suicide bombing during Palm Sunday Mass that killed dozens; it endures as both a place of worship and of memory.
s: Seat of the Coptic papacy, marked by tragedy in 2017
_facts: Historical seat of the Pope of Alexandria, head of the Coptic Orthodox Church
Target of a suicide bombing on Palm Sunday, 9 April 2017, one of twin attacks that killed at least 43 people
Principal Coptic cathedral in Alexandria

w: Inaugurated in 2003 inside a renovated Italian-style palace on what used to be Rue Fouad, this museum spans the full sweep of Egyptian history, pharaonic through Islamic to modern, inside a single building. Its former life as the United States consulate is just one more layer in a structure that keeps being repurposed.
s: Egypt's history under one roof, in a former consulate
_facts: Museum inaugurated 31 December 2003 by Hosni Mubarak, on Tariq Al-Horreya Street (former Rue Fouad)
Housed in a renovated Italian-style palace, formerly the United States consulate
Covers Egyptian history across pharaonic, Greco-Roman, Coptic, Islamic and modern periods

w: Standing on Nabi Daniel Street, this synagogue is one of the last visible traces of Alexandria's once-substantial Jewish community, a population that has dwindled to almost nothing over the past century. The building's scale still hints at the size of the congregation that used to fill it every week.
s: A grand synagogue for a community nearly gone
_facts: Synagogue located at 69 Nabi Daniel Street, Alexandria
Serves what remains of Alexandria's historic Jewish community
Named for the prophet Elijah (Eliyahu Hanavi)

w: This is where Alexandria keeps the evidence of its Greek and Roman centuries, more than 40,000 sculptures, mosaics, carved woodwork and coins, pulled from digs across the city and beyond. It is less flashy than the newer museums but deeper, a working archive of everything Alexandria used to be before Islam arrived.
s: 40,000 objects from the city's Greek and Roman past
_facts: Archaeological museum in Alexandria with a collection of over 40,000 objects
Holdings include sculptures, mosaics, woodwork and coins from Alexandria's Greek and Roman periods

w: Cleopatra VII commissioned this temple to honour Julius Caesar or Mark Antony, only for Augustus to finish it and rededicate it to himself after defeating them both. Converted into a church, it was where a mob murdered the philosopher Hypatia in 415. Its obelisks, Cleopatra's Needles, now stand in London and New York.
s: Cleopatra built it; a mob murdered a philosopher there
_facts: Ancient temple conceived by Cleopatra VII, completed and rededicated to himself by Augustus
Converted to a Christian church in the late 4th century; philosopher Hypatia murdered there by a mob in 415
Its two obelisks, Cleopatra's Needles, now stand in Central Park, New York, and on the Thames Embankment, London

w: Sitting on the promontory once the island of Pharos, this is the oldest royal Egyptian palace still in use, built under the Muhammad Ali dynasty and still an official presidential residence. It overlooks Alexandria's western harbour from a site with centuries of history beneath its foundations.
s: The oldest royal Egyptian palace still in active use
_facts: Palace on the Mediterranean coast in the Ras el-Tin quarter, built on the former site of the island of Pharos
Royal palace of the Muhammad Ali Dynasty; oldest royal Egyptian palace still in use
Registered as Islamic and Coptic antiquities in 2015; used as an official presidential residence

w: The cornerstone went down in 1847 and it took nine years to finish this trilateral basilica, built in a neo-Gothic style more associated with northern Europe than the Mediterranean. It has served the Greek community of Alexandria ever since and remains the seat of the Patriarchate of Alexandria and All Africa.
s: A neo-Gothic cathedral, nine years in the building
_facts: Also known as the Cathedral of the Annunciation; cornerstone laid 16 November 1847, completed 1856
Built in neo-Gothic rather than neo-Byzantine style; serves the Greek community of Alexandria
Ecclesiastical seat of the Patriarchate of Alexandria and All Africa

w: Built between 1918 and 1921 and inaugurated as the Teatro Mohamed Ali in front of King Fouad I, this Renaissance Revival theatre seats 1,200 and still stages opera and concerts today. It picked up its current name, honouring composer Sayed Darwish, after the 1952 revolution swept away the monarchy that had opened it.
s: A 1,200-seat opera house that opened for a king
_facts: Renaissance Revival opera house built 1918-1921, designed by Georges Parcq
Inaugurated as the Teatro Mohamed Ali in the presence of King Fouad I
Renamed Alexandria Opera House / Sayed Darwish Theatre after the 1952 revolution

w: This museum occupies the former palace of Princess Fatma Al-Zahra in the Zizenia neighbourhood, its halls holding a collection of jewels and jewelry from the Muhammad Ali dynasty alongside nineteenth-century paintings and decorative art. First opened in 1986, it reopened in 2010 after renovation.
s: A dynasty's jewels, kept in a princess's old palace
_facts: Art and history museum in the former palace of Princess Fatma Al-Zahra, Zizenia neighbourhood
Collection of jewels and jewelry belonging to the Muhammad Ali Dynasty, plus 19th-century paintings and decorative arts
First inaugurated 24 October 1986; reopened April 2010 after renovation

w: Also known as the Terbana Mosque, this modest building sits on Faransa Street in the El Gomrok quarter, part of Alexandria's old town where fragments of the city's Ottoman-era Islamic architecture survive among the modern blocks. It is named after Ibrahim Terbana, whose own story is otherwise mostly lost to time.
s: A mosque tucked down a street named for France
_facts: Mosque in the El Gomrok neighbourhood of Alexandria, on Faransa Street
Also known as the Mosque of Ibrahim Terbana

w: The whole surrounding neighbourhood took its name from the Attarin Market that once anchored it, a bazaar famous across the region for spices and perfumes since the Islamic conquest of Egypt. Traders here supplied households throughout the eastern Mediterranean, and the district still carries the trade's name today.
s: The old spice souk that named its own district
_facts: El Attarin neighbourhood named after the historic Attarin Market at its centre
Market was famous for the spice and perfume trade, especially since the Islamic conquest of Egypt
